name: The Fortingall Yew
age_estimate: estimates range from roughly 2,000 to 5,000 years

location.address: Fortingall churchyard, Fortingall, Perthshire PH15 2NQ, Scotland

access: Free. Stands inside the churchyard, behind a low wall erected in 1785 to protect it from souvenir-taking; the gate in the wall is kept locked so it cannot be touched, but it is easily viewed and photographed from the churchyard path, which is open in daylight hours.
transport: No station; Fortingall is a small village about 8 miles / 20-25 minutes by car west of Aberfeldy, Perthshire. No regular public bus serves the village itself.
verify_notes:
ALIVE: yes, well documented. Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh reported in Oct/Nov 2015 that a branch had begun bearing berries (a male yew turning partially female), which is itself proof of a living, physiologically active tree, not just a standing trunk; the story is carried by RBGE's own site (stories.rbge.org.uk/archives/17622) and BBC News (2 Nov 2015). Scotland's Yew Tree Heritage Initiative (scotlands-yew-trees.org, page last modified 2021) independently describes it as still standing and still of interest, 'recently showing signs of changing sex'. A 2019 Scotsman piece reports concern from the local Tree Warden about tourists pulling off branches for souvenirs, i.e. still standing and still visited that year. No fresher (2023-2026) dated source was found in this pass, but nothing suggests decline; it is a slow-growing yew inside a walled, protected churchyard enclosure, not a fragile specimen.
AGE: genuinely disputed among real sources, not a data error. Forestry and Land Scotland (cited by Wikipedia) states 5,000 years. Bevan-Jones (2004), the standard academic reference on ancient yews, gives 2,000-3,000 years, noting it may date to a post-Roman Christian site (~1,500 years) at the low end. Deliver the full disputed range rather than picking a side; nobody can rewind the trunk since its heartwood rotted out and was recorded hollow/fragmented as far back as 1769-1833, which is exactly why no ring count exists and never will.
GIRTH: trunk girth was recorded in 1769 at 52 feet (about 15.85 m) by Daines Barrington, and again by Thomas Pennant shortly after at 56.5 feet; these are HISTORICAL measurements of the once-continuous trunk before it fragmented into several separate stems from heartwood decay (noted by 1770). Recording girth_cm=1585 (52 ft) as the documented historical figure, not a current single-stem measurement; say so explicitly, since the tree today reads as a grove of several stems rather than one trunk of that girth.
REMARKABLE / DESTINATION TEST: yes, unambiguously. Widely called one of the oldest trees in Britain and possibly Europe (excluding clonal root systems like Old Tjikko); it has its own substantial Wikipedia page, an urban legend tying it to Pontius Pilate's birth (historically debunked but part of why people specifically travel here), and its DNA is being propagated by the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh's 'Yew Conservation Hedge Project' specifically because of its singular fame. People plan trips to rural Perthshire for this one tree; it passes easily.
COORDINATES: Wikipedia infobox gives 56.59823,-4.05093 (church/tree, sourced to OS mapping); the brief's coordinate 56.59794,-4.05216 is about 90m away, likely a looser Commons-category pin. Using the Wikipedia infobox figure as the more precise one; both point at the same small churchyard so this does not change location_precision.
curation_status flagged for the age spread, not for existence or location, both of which are solid.

name: Old Tjikko
age_estimate: root system approximately 9,550 years old; the visible trunk is only a few centuries old

location.address: Fulufjället National Park, on the mountain plateau above Njupeskär, Älvdalen Municipality, Dalarna, Sweden
location.neighbourhood: Fulufjället mountain plateau, reached via the Njupeskär trail

access: Free (Swedish national parks charge no entry fee). Reached only on foot: a marked, self-guided hiking trail (orange markers on stones and signage) climbs from the Njupeskärsstugan area up onto the mountain plateau, roughly 7-9 km round trip depending on the route chosen, gaining real elevation onto open fell terrain. No guide or booking is required, but hikers must stay on the marked path because the mountain heath vegetation is fragile, and the route can still be under snow into early summer. Not a casual stroll: sturdy footwear and weather-appropriate clothing for exposed alpine terrain are needed.
transport: No public transport reaches the trailhead. Nearest access is by car to the Naturum Fulufjället visitor centre / Njupeskär car park (near Sarna/Mora area, Dalarna), then the hike above. Allow a full half-day round trip from the car park.
verify_notes:
CRITICAL DISTINCTION, must survive into the story: the ~9,550-year figure is the age of the CLONAL ROOT SYSTEM, carbon-dated (samples returned 375, 5,660, 9,000 and 9,550 years before 2008, per Umea University). The visible trunk standing today is NOT that old: Wikipedia (citing the discovering researchers, Leif Kullman and Lisa Oberg of Umea University) and the Swedish national park's own page both say the trunk any visitor sees is only a few centuries old (park page: 'nagra hundra ar', a few hundred years), because the tree has survived by vegetative cloning/layering: a trunk dies back after roughly 600 years and a new one sprouts from the still-living root system. So age_min/age_max here both record the root system's dated age (9550) since that is the tree's verified and famous claim, but verify_notes must carry the trunk/root split explicitly so the writer never states the visible tree as 9,550 years old.
ALIVE: yes, and recently confirmed. The Swedish national park authority's own page (Naturvardsverket / Lansstyrelsen Dalarna, live page fetched this pass) reports that in February 2023 a winter storm snapped off about one metre of Old Tjikko's top, and that broken top is now on display at the Naturum Fulufjallet visitor centre. This is dated, official, first-party evidence the tree was alive and standing as of Feb 2023 (a storm cannot break the top off a dead/absent tree), and nothing suggests it died from that damage; spruces regularly survive lost tops. Also: in July 2024 the Stockholm art studio Goldin+Senneby (Dezeen, 1 July 2024) built a climate-controlled installation in Malmo housing a clone grown from grafted twigs cut from Old Tjikko's own top branches, meaning live plant material was being taken from the tree as recently as 2024. Two independent, dated confirmations of life within the last three years.
SPECIES/GIRTH: no girth is published anywhere found; the visible stem is described as slender rather than massive; height is 5 m per Wikipedia (sourced to CNN, 2008), unchanged in any newer source found. girth_cm left null rather than guessed.
SOURCE AGREEMENT: Wikipedia (Good Article, heavily sourced to BBC 2008, CNN 2008, National Geographic 2008, Umea University press release 2008, and Dezeen 2024) and the Swedish national park's own official page agree on every fact checked: species, location, the clonal nature, the age figures, and the storm damage account (the storm/top-break detail exists on the park's Swedish page but was not in the Wikipedia raw wikitext fetched, which is a gap in Wikipedia's coverage rather than a contradiction).
ACCESS: settled directly from the national park authority's own visitor page, not from a search summary. Self-guided marked trail from Njupeskarsstugan, no permission or booking needed, roughly 7-9 km round trip over exposed mountain terrain (cross-checked against Komoot/Outdooractive/AllTrails route lengths, which cluster around 6.9-8.6 km depending on start point). location_precision set to approximate: the coordinate is the Wikipedia/Commons-sourced pin for the tree on the plateau, but this is remote alpine terrain without a street address or a mapped structure to confirm the pin against, and the park's own text points to it only via trail markers rather than a stated coordinate.
DESTINATION TEST: yes, clearly. Marketed globally and by Sweden's own national park authority as 'the world's oldest tree', Wikipedia article exists in 32 languages, requires a dedicated multi-hour hike into a national park specifically to see it rather than being a park amenity encountered in passing. People plan trips to rural Dalarna for this exact tree.

place: Santa María del Tule, Oaxaca, Mexico
name: El Árbol del Tule
age_estimate: widely reported as roughly 1,400 to 1,600 years old on growth-rate grounds, though popular sources often round it to 'over 2,000'

location.address: Church grounds (atrio of the Templo de Santa María de la Asunción), town center of Santa María del Tule, Oaxaca, Mexico, on the road toward Mitla, about 9 km east of Oaxaca city
location.neighbourhood: Santa María del Tule town center, church courtyard

access: Small paid entrance fee to the church courtyard where the tree stands (per Planeta.com's visitor guide); open daily as a standard tourist site in the town center, not restricted. Local festivities are held around it, notably the second Monday of October.
transport: Second-class buses run every 10 minutes from Oaxaca city's second-class bus station direct to Santa María del Tule; also reachable by a roughly half-hour bike ride or short taxi/collectivo from Oaxaca city centre.
verify_notes:
ALIVE: yes, confirmed recently and formally. Ciudadania Express (dated 3 October 2025) reports the Oaxaca state government's Fourth State Declaration for Natural Heritage event held AT the tree, where officials performed sonic tomography and a formal health assessment as part of certifying it and 40 other trees as protected Notable/Historic Trees; officials called it 'a natural and spiritual monument of Mexico and the world'. A health assessment and a public ceremony at the tree in October 2025 is strong, dated, first-party-adjacent evidence it is alive and under active official monitoring, not evidence of decline. Older reporting (a 1990 Press-Courier piece cited by Wikipedia, and Planeta.com's ongoing coverage) documents chronic water-table stress from a nearby highway, irrigation and aquifer depletion (Planeta: water table can drop over 6 m in dry season; a 2022 drought reportedly forced a choice between watering the town or the tree, per general search results not independently confirmed this pass). This is a real, long-running THREAT, not evidence the tree is currently dead or dying; it should read as an honest caveat about a stressed but living tree, not a death flag.
SOURCE DISAGREEMENT ON GIRTH: Wikipedia/Gymnosperm Database, citing a laser-assisted 2005 measurement, gives trunk circumference as 42.0 m (diameter 14.05 m raw, or 9.38 m when the heavy buttressing is smoothed out, which the Gymnosperm Database treats as the fairer comparison to other 'stoutest tree' claimants like giant sequoias at 8.90 m). Planeta.com states circumference as 54 m; a widely circulated set of numbers (seen in this pass's search results, not independently verified on a primary page) gives 45 m circumference and a 14.36 m diameter. Recording girth_cm as 4200 (the sourced 2005 measurement with a citable methodology) and flagging the tree because of this real, unresolved spread; the writer should say 'roughly 42 to 54 metres depending on the source' rather than pick one, per the register/measurement-conflict rule.
HEIGHT: Wikipedia's 2005 laser measurement gives 35.4 m, shorter than earlier (pre-2005) estimates of 41-43 m cited in the same article; a 2025 search-summary figure of 'more than 40 m' could not be verified on a fetched primary page (search-summary rule: not used). Height not recorded in the structured field given this spread; the writer may use the sourced 35.4 m 2005 figure with a note that older estimates ran higher.
AGE: also disputed and this pass follows Wikipedia's own hierarchy of estimates rather than inventing a synthesis: local Zapotec oral history plus the best scientific growth-rate estimate (Conzatti, 1921, cited by Wikipedia) converge on roughly 1,400-1,600 years; wider published estimates run from 1,200 to 3,000 years, with an outlier claim of 6,000 sometimes repeated; popular press today (ciudadania-express and others) commonly rounds this to 'over 2,000 years' or even 'milenario' without citing a method. age_min/age_max set to the wide 1200-3000 published range rather than either extreme; age_estimate names the more defensible 1,400-1,600 figure while flagging the discrepancy for the writer.
SINGLE TREE, NOT A GROVE: DNA testing (Dorado et al. 1996, and Hall 1990, both cited by Wikipedia) confirmed it is genetically one individual despite its huge multi-lobed trunk once being mistaken for several trees fused together; this matters for the collectible-point test.
DESTINATION TEST: yes, unambiguously. Called the stoutest tree trunk in the world by most accounts (a claim actively contested only by giant sequoias on a smoothed-trunk basis), was on UNESCO's tentative World Heritage list 2001-2013, and draws dedicated day-trippers from Oaxaca city specifically to see it; it is a famous specimen tourists travel to Oaxaca partly in order to see, not a park amenity.
COORDINATES: brief's coordinate (17.04662,-96.63346) matches the church/town-centre location Wikipedia describes; treating as confirmed given the tree is a single unmistakable landmark in a small town's central plaza, not a case needing satellite corroboration.

name: Tāne Mahuta
age_estimate: estimated 1,250 to 2,500 years old; age is not precisely measurable

location.address: Tāne Mahuta Walk car park, State Highway 12, Waipoua Forest, Northland, New Zealand
location.neighbourhood: Waipoua Forest, signposted directly off SH12

access: Free. A short, easy, wheelchair- and buggy-accessible boardwalk (166 m, about 5 minutes one way) from a roadside car park directly off State Highway 12, open 9am-3pm daily (hours can shift seasonally, check DOC's page). A mandatory shoe/gear cleaning station sits at the entrance to stop kauri dieback disease spreading; visitors must stay on the boardwalk at all times to protect the tree's shallow, disease-vulnerable roots.
transport: No public transport; reached by car on SH12. Roughly 65 km / under an hour from Dargaville to the south, 18 km from Omapere to the north.
verify_notes:
ALIVE: yes, strongly and recently confirmed. New Zealand's Department of Conservation (official government agency managing the site) issued a dated media release on 21 December 2024 announcing Tane Mahuta's walking track reopened that day after a dawn blessing by Te Roroa (the local iwi/tribal guardians), following conservation works (new raised boardwalk, bridge and viewing platform) as part of the ongoing 'Rakau Rangatira' project between Te Roroa and DOC to protect the tree from kauri dieback disease. The track had been closed since 30 September 2024 specifically for this protective work, not because the tree was in danger of dying. DOC's own current visitor page (fetched this pass) lists live 2026 opening hours (9am-3pm daily), confirming the site is an actively maintained, currently open attraction. Search results (not independently fetched, so treated as leads only) describe Tane Mahuta as still free of kauri dieback infection itself as of the mid-2020s, though the pathogen has been detected within about 60 m of the tree, which is exactly why DOC built the new boardwalk and wash stations. Net picture: alive, actively protected, and the subject of continuous, well-funded conservation effort, not a tree in doubt.
SPECIES/GIRTH/HEIGHT: Wikipedia's infobox figures (girth 15.44 m, height 45.2 m, trunk volume 255.5 m3) come from a 2002 measurement by dendrologist Dr Robert Van Pelt (University of Washington) and are the most rigorously sourced set found. DOC's own current visitor page instead lists trunk girth 13.77 m and total height 51.2 m, an unexplained difference from Van Pelt's 2002 figures (page does not give a measurement date). Recording girth_cm as 1544 (Van Pelt 2002, cited methodology) and flagging this discrepancy for the writer; either figure supports 'one of the largest living kauri trees' regardless.
AGE: unmeasurable directly (no dendrochronology on a species this size/age is practical without killing it), so all figures are estimates; Wikipedia gives the commonly cited range 1,250-2,500 years. Recording that range rather than a false precise midpoint.
COORDINATES: brief's pin (-35.60735,173.52201) is roughly 700m south of Wikipedia's infobox coordinate (35.60111 S, 173.5272 E, i.e. -35.60111,173.5272); using the Wikipedia figure as it is sourced to a German Wikipedia landmark-type coordinate specifically for the tree, and DOC's own page places the walk directly off SH12 at a signposted car park matching that area. location_precision confirmed given DOC operates a single, unambiguous, signposted short boardwalk to one specific tree.
DESTINATION TEST: yes, overwhelmingly. Named 'Lord of the Forest', the largest living kauri known, formally partnered in 2009 with Japan's Jomon Sugi as a sister ancient tree, subject of dedicated government conservation projects and a public blessing ceremony, and one of New Zealand's most recognised natural landmarks; people build entire Northland/Far North itineraries around visiting this specific tree.
DESTINATION-TEST NOTE ON THE FOREST: Waipoua Forest holds several famous kauri (this tree, Te Matua Ngahere, Four Sisters, Yakas Kauri), so this also functions as a walkable cluster; see companion entries and the blocked note on Four Sisters. PIN CORRECTED 2026-09-03 by the dispatching session: the latitude was delivered without its minus sign, which put a New Zealand kauri in the Pacific east of Japan. Longitude and the rest are as delivered.

name: Te Matua Ngahere
age_estimate: commonly cited as exceeding 2,000 years; published estimates range much wider and are unverifiable

location.address: Te Matua Ngahere Walk, accessed from the Kauri Walks car park, State Highway 12, Waipoua Forest, Northland, New Zealand
location.neighbourhood: Waipoua Forest, about 4 km / 3 minutes' drive south of the Tane Mahuta car park

access: Free. A 730 m, roughly 20-minute walk on a well-maintained, partly boardwalked track from the Kauri Walks car park off SH12, open 9am-4pm daily. Ends at a viewing platform about 10 m from the trunk; visitors must stay on the track and use the mandatory boot-cleaning wash stations to protect the tree from kauri dieback disease.
transport: No public transport; reached by car on SH12, about 61 km from Dargaville and 21 km from Omapere. Shares the same car park area as the Four Sisters and Yakas Kauri walks, though those two are currently closed (see fam blocked note).
verify_notes:
ALIVE and REACHABLE NOW: DOC's own current visitor page for this exact walk (fetched this pass, live 2026 content) states it is 'open 9 am to 4 pm daily' and gives full walking directions from the Kauri Walks car park; this is the same live, actively maintained government tourism page used to confirm Tane Mahuta (fam_004), from the same forest management programme (Rakau Rangatira / Te Roroa and DOC). No dieback infection of this specific tree is reported in any source found this pass, and its own dedicated wash station and boardwalk are the standard DOC dieback-prevention infrastructure applied here as at Tane Mahuta.
DAMAGE HISTORY, not a death flag: in July 2007 a large rata tree that had been growing epiphytically on top of Te Matua Ngahere was brought down by a severe winter storm, taking the kauri's central leader and several branches with it; both Wikipedia and the original NZ Herald report ('Storm takes heart of forest king', 13 July 2007) describe this as having shortened the tree's expected lifespan by an estimated few hundred years, not as having killed it. The tree has continued to be a functioning, visited DOC walk in every source found since, including the live 2026 page.
SPECIES/GIRTH/HEIGHT: Wikipedia and DOC's own current page agree closely: trunk girth 16.41 m, trunk height 10.21 m, total height 29.9 m, trunk volume 208.1 m3. Wikipedia flags that these are 1971 New Zealand Forest Service measurements, not recent ones, and points to the New Zealand Tree Register for anything more current; DOC's own 2026 page still repeats the same 1971 figures verbatim, so this pass is using the one set both sources agree on rather than chasing a possibly-updated register figure under the time box.
AGE: genuinely unmeasurable and widely disputed across real sources: various published estimates run 1,200-2,000 years, 2,000-3,000 years, or as much as 4,000 years, with 'over 1,500' also cited; DOC's own current page states 'estimated to exceed 2,000 years'. Recording the full published spread (1200-4000) rather than picking one, per the register/estimate-conflict rule; age_estimate uses DOC's own current framing ('exceeding 2,000 years') as the headline claim since it is the live, official figure, while verify_notes carries the dispute for the writer.
COORDINATES: brief's pin (-35.60725,173.52897) is very close to Wikipedia's infobox coordinate (35.60750 S, 173.52861 E / -35.60750,173.52861), within about 40 m, well inside the margin of a single named walk with one viewing platform; treating as confirmed.
DESTINATION TEST: yes. Second-largest living kauri known and, by most accounts, the stoutest-girthed tree in New Zealand; Wikipedia calls it, with Tane Mahuta, one of the two most famous trees in the country, revered by Maori and watched over by local guardians; DOC reports roughly 50,000 visitors a year specifically to this tree. People visit Waipoua Forest to see this tree and Tane Mahuta together as a pair; it stands on its own destination merits as well.
CLUSTER NOTE: this tree and Tane Mahuta sit about 4 km apart by road (3-minute drive), each with its own short walk from its own car park; a visitor drives between them rather than walking, which the story should say honestly rather than imply one long forest walk connects them. PIN CORRECTED 2026-09-03 by the dispatching session: the latitude was delivered without its minus sign, which put a New Zealand kauri in the Pacific east of Japan. Longitude and the rest are as delivered.

name: Kongeegen (the King Oak)
age_estimate: estimated 1,500 to 2,000 years old, based on a 1965 tree-ring investigation

location.address: Jægerspris Nordskov (Jægerspris North Forest), north of Strandvejen, near Jægerspris, Sjælland, Denmark
location.neighbourhood: Jægerspris Nordskov forest, managed by Kong Frederik den Syvendes Stiftelse (the Jægerspris Slot estate foundation)

access: Free, publicly accessible forest, but the tree itself is fenced off: visitors may not walk or ride up to the trunk, only view it from outside the protective fence, per the managing foundation's own current website. Reachable on foot through the North Forest; no ticket or booking needed.
transport: No train station in Jægerspris; reached by car or bicycle via Strandvejen north of the town, then on foot into the forest. Nearest larger town/station is Frederikssund, a short drive away.
verify_notes:
ALIVE: yes, confirmed by the most authoritative and most current source available: Kong Frederik den Syvendes Stiftelse, the foundation that owns and manages Jaegerspris Slot and its forest, on its own website, page last modified 2026-09-02 (one day before this pass, per the page's own schema.org dateModified metadata). Its own words: 'I aarhundreder har de overlevet storme og skovhugst, og det aeldste trae, Kongeegen, lever stadig' (For centuries they have survived storms and logging, and the oldest tree, Kongeegen, is STILL ALIVE). The same page describes ongoing recent maintenance: 'Stiftelsen har i nyere tid opsat nye stoetter' (the Foundation has in recent times put up new supports) so the tree 'forhaabentligt i mange aar endnu kan bevare sin vaerdighed' (can hopefully preserve its dignity for many more years). The Danish Dendrological Society's own tree register (dendron.dk, Individual_ID=418) independently lists Status as 'Levende, svag' (Living, weak) as of its most recent report (13-12-2008; older than the foundation's page but concordant, and a hollow ancient oak reported 'weak' in 2008 and still being actively supported and discussed as alive in 2026 is an internally consistent story, not a contradiction).
CRITICAL FINDING (matches what the brief flagged to check): the SAME foundation page states plainly that the other two famous oaks in this forest are DEAD, both with specific dates, so this pass is NOT delivering them; see the blocked entries for Storkeegen and Snoegen with the exact quotes.
AGE: Wikipedia states a 1965 scientific tree-ring investigation gave an estimated age of 1,500-2,000 years, possibly the oldest living oak in northern Europe. The foundation's own page independently states the identical range, 'en alder paa 1500-2000 aar', and adds the striking framing that it may have sprouted around year 0. Both sources plausibly derive from the same 1965 study lineage, so this is treated as one estimate corroborated twice rather than two independent datings; recorded as a DERIVED estimate (tree-ring based), not invented.
GIRTH: two figures exist. The foundation's page gives the tree's historical PEAK measurement, diameter 4 m / circumference 14 m ('Paa sit hoejeste havde Kongeegens stamme en diameter paa 4 meter og en omkreds paa 14 meter'), explicitly framed as its largest-ever size, since the trunk has since partly collapsed (last main branch broke off 1973, since when half the shell and a side branch have fallen). The Danish Dendrological Society's register gives a more precise current figure, omkreds 12.55 m (girth_cm=1255), which is what is recorded here as the more current, precisely-sourced measurement; the writer should note the tree was once larger before storm/decay losses.
STRUCTURE: now a hollow shell rather than a solid trunk ('traeet stadig staar som en olding, understoettet og med aaben stamme', standing like an old man, supported and with an open/hollow trunk). This is normal for ancient oaks and not itself a death signal; the foundation explicitly frames the crown as 'forbavsende godt' (surprisingly good) for the tree's age.
HISTORY worth keeping for the writer: named for King Frederik VII, who lived at Jaegerspris Slot 1854-1863 with Countess Danner and who had the first support pillars installed; legend says the king and countess could sit on horseback side by side inside the hollow trunk. A grafted clone, called 'Danneregen', was planted in Jaegerspris Slotspark in 1986 by Prince Henrik of Denmark, using material taken from Kongeegen itself.
DESTINATION TEST: yes. Widely cited as northern Europe's oldest oak / possibly oldest living oak, has its own Wikipedia page and dedicated foundation web page, and is the specific reason 'De tusindaarige ege' (The Thousand-Year Oaks) is a named forest attraction; visitors come to Nordskoven specifically to see this named tree, not incidentally.
COORDINATES: three independent sources agree closely: Wikipedia infobox (55.9103,11.9892 from DMS), dendron.dk's own Google-Earth-sourced reading (55.91035,11.98927), and the brief's own pin (55.91031,11.98911), all within about 15 m of each other for a single fenced, named tree in a forest; confirmed.

name: The Stelmužė Oak
age_estimate: at least 1,500 years old, possibly as much as 2,000

location.address: Former Stelmužė Manor park, next to the Stelmužė Church of St Anne, Stelmužė village, Zarasai district, Lithuania
location.neighbourhood: Stelmužė village, in the old manor park beside the wooden church

access: A protected national natural monument standing in a public village setting beside a historic church (Lithuania's oldest surviving wooden church, built in the 17th century); no source found in this pass mentions an entry fee or restricted hours, consistent with it being an open-air village landmark rather than a ticketed site. Not independently confirmed with opening hours from an official tourism page this pass (visitzarasai.lt's specific page returned a 404 and lithuania.travel's page did not yield fetchable content in the time available); flagging this as a gap for a future pass or the writer to double check rather than asserting hours we do not have.
transport: No train station; Stelmužė is a small village in Zarasai district, north-eastern Lithuania, reached by car. Zarasai town is the nearest larger centre.
verify_notes:
ALIVE: yes, and recently confirmed. Tree of the Year (treeoftheyear.org, the international arboricultural body behind the annual European Tree of the Year contest, which the Stelmuze Oak entered/won recognition in 2017 per a separate page on the same site) published a dedicated article dated 8 January 2026 describing ongoing, current conservation work: condition monitoring by specialists, branch supports to prevent structural collapse, and continued threat assessment. This is a dated (8 months before this pass), independent, specialist-organisation source describing active, present-tense stewardship of a living tree, not a retrospective about a dead one. Wikipedia (citing the Universal Lithuanian Encyclopedia) independently corroborates: 'in early March 2021 new supports were installed, one branch broke on 31 March 2021', and names a Czech arborist, Martin Nemec, who has monitored and maintained the tree's condition since 2005 with a long-term maintenance plan. Two independent sources, both describing active current-day arboricultural care, agree the tree stands and is being kept alive.
CONDITION, not a death flag: the tree is hollow (its inner trunk has decayed and is gone, which is exactly why 'exact age measurements are difficult' per Wikipedia), heavily colonised by fungi and moss, and only side branches remain alive rather than a full crown; this is described consistently across sources as the expected state of a very old, actively managed veteran oak, not as an oak in terminal decline.
AGE: unmeasurable precisely because the trunk's interior is gone (no ring count possible); both sources give the same DERIVED range, 'at least 1,500, possibly up to 2,000 years', making it the oldest oak in Lithuania and one of the oldest in Europe. Treated as one estimate rather than two independent datings since both plausibly trace to the same standing assessment (referenced via the Universal Lithuanian Encyclopedia).
GIRTH/HEIGHT: Wikipedia gives multiple measurement points depending on where the trunk is measured: 13 m circumference / 3.5 m diameter at its widest point, versus 9.58 m circumference / 2.8 m diameter at waist (breast) height, the more standard forestry measurement point; 23 m total height. Recording girth_cm as 1300 (the widest-point figure, which is the one most sources quote as headline) but flagging that a narrower, more standard breast-height figure of 958 cm also exists and the writer should pick the framing that matches how other trees in our database are measured.
HISTORY worth keeping for the writer: during restoration work a rifle and a human skeleton were found inside the hollow trunk, believed (per Tree of the Year) to be a French soldier from Napoleon's 1812 retreat from Russia. The tree appeared on a 2013 Lithuanian 2-litai commemorative coin and on postage stamps, and an offspring grown from its acorns was planted in the National Revival Oak Grove beside the birthplace of Jonas Basanavicius (the Lithuanian 'Patriarch of the Nation'), alongside offspring of other historically significant Lithuanian oaks.
DUPLICATE LEAD CHECKED, per the brief's own instruction: data/leads/_famous-lithuania.json holds two lead rows at the identical coordinate (55.82986,26.2173), one named 'Stelmuze oak' and one named 'Quercus in Lithuania' (the latter's photo list includes a Stelmuze oak Commons image, 2017_Stelmuze_oak_LT.jpg, confirming it is the same tree mis-split by the automated famous-trees sweep). Confirmed as one tree, delivering once, not twice; the lead file itself was left untouched since deduplicating it is not this pass's job, only flagging it here as the brief asked.
DESTINATION TEST: yes. Lithuania's oldest and most iconic individual tree, a genuine national symbol (currency and stamp imagery), the subject of a dedicated European-level conservation body's coverage, and its own historical intrigue (the Napoleonic-era remains found inside it); it is a place people specifically travel to rural north-eastern Lithuania to see.
